source.title_on_document: Who Is the Best Helper for University Students' Mathematical Creativity? A Quasi-Experimental Study of Human–ChatGPT, Human–Google, and Human–Human Co-Creation

supplement.where: Online Supporting Information of the Wiley article: 'Appendix. Supporting document.' (PDF p. 16). The article DOI is 10.1002/cae.70100 (p. 1); no supplement-specific URL is printed. The saved PDF has no embedded files.
supplement.holds: According to the main text, the supplement contains MCT scoring reference tables (p. 6, Section 5) and exploratory correlation tables; Appendix Tables A1 and A3 are named on pp. 11-12, Sections 7.4-7.5. The appendix itself was not obtained, so other contents and any additional statistics remain unverified. All creativity statistics recorded in this form are printed in the main PDF (p. 7, Table 3; pp. 7-8, Section 6.1).

paper_design_summary: Chinese university student volunteers completed a solo baseline task followed by four open-ended mathematical creativity tasks with a lottery-assigned partner: ChatGPT, Google Search, or a human peer (230 participants in groups of 60, 60, and 110; the peer group comprised 55 dyads; pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1-3.2 and Table 1). The creativity analyses include 60 ChatGPT participants and 60 Google participants; the peer arm's t (54) tests imply 55 observations, but their representation of its 110 members is not explained (pp. 7-8, Section 6.1). Two scorers coded submitted solutions for flexibility, fluency, and originality (pp. 6-7, Section 5).

studies.label: Mathematical creativity tasks with ChatGPT, Google Search, or a human peer

assignment.what_was_assigned: Co-creation partner for the MCT: ChatGPT, Google Search only, or a human peer (dyad). In the human–human arm, pairs were also formed at random, and one member (person A) led.
assignment.quote: Each student was randomly assigned to one of the three experimental conditions (human–ChatGPT group, human–Google group, or human–human group) using a lottery system.

arms.name: Human–ChatGPT
arms.description: Student solves the MCT with ChatGPT open in a single browser tab on a PC with identical settings; told that ChatGPT responds to prompts, that more background gives more accurate responses, that responses can be refined, and that images or documents can be uploaded.

arms.name: Human–Google
arms.description: Student solves the MCT with Google Search only; all other AI tools and search engines blocked.

arms.name: Human–human
arms.description: Randomly formed student pairs (110 participants in 55 dyads); person A led the task and person B took a supportive, passive role without completing work independently (p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.2). The creativity tests imply 55 observations, but the source does not specify whether these are joint dyad scores or scores for person A alone; the analyzed-person count is therefore unconfirmed (pp. 7-8, Section 6.1).

participants.exclusions: The paper states: 'Each participant completed all the required tasks, and none were excluded' (p. 3, Section 3.1). The lottery-formed groups are reported as 60, 60, and 110 people (p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 4, Table 1); these are retained as the reported assignment-group counts, although no separate tally at the draw is printed. The ChatGPT and Google arms each analyzed 60 people, supported by their group sizes, the no-exclusion statement, and t (59) tests (pp. 7-8, Section 6.1). For the peer arm, t (54) is consistent with 55 observations, and the three-group F (2, 172) with 175 observations (usual t-test df + 1 and ANOVA residual df + 3 groups). Those observation counts are inferred from the printed degrees of freedom, not separately reported analyzed-person totals. The source does not explain whether each peer score represents both members jointly or person A alone, or how the individually completed baselines enter that arm's analysis. Accordingly, the peer and overall analyzed-person counts are null; neither 230 participants nor 175 implied observations is treated as a confirmed overall analyzed-person count. This is an unresolved mapping of people to scores, not evidence of 55 exclusions. Table 1's demographic comparisons use F (2, 227), consistent with all 230 participants.
participants.who: Chinese university student volunteers from sciences, liberal arts, and engineering, recruited across majors through the counselor and rewarded with a few credits; no specific mathematics background (p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 4, Table 1)
participants.quote: A total of 230 Chinese university students participated in this study.
participants.locator: p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 4, Table 1; pp. 7-8, Section 6.1 and p. 7, Table 3

ai_tool.how_used: Free use of ChatGPT in one browser tab as a co-creation partner while solving the MCT. Students were told how to prompt, refine responses, and upload images or documents, and all arms were encouraged to draw inspiration from their partner. The web browser was available for searches, but no one used it.

task.description: Mathematical creativity tasks (MCT) adapted from Lee and Seo: four open-ended tasks asking for as many answers as possible (2 cm² figures on a 4 × 4 grid; methods to measure the dispersion of marbles; properties of water in a tilted rectangular prism; shapes sharing features with shape A). Baseline: a number-pyramid task (Table 2) solved alone before the partner phase.
task.duration: Whole study 80 min (SD = 7) in human–ChatGPT, 70 min (SD = 5) in human–Google, 68 min (SD = 7.8) in human–human (p. 3)

outcomes.name: MCT flexibility
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of correct answer categories in each task, summed over the four tasks. Answers were marked correct or wrong and then categorized by hand by two scorers (Cohen's kappa 0.85 on 18 pre-study samples, above 0.91 on the remaining data; discrepancies reanalyzed to 100% agreement). Table 3 gives raw arm means; the mixed ANOVA (condition × time, baseline vs MCT) uses z-standardized scores. ANCOVA test of prior mathematical competence: F (2, 171) = 0.02, p = 0.880 (p. 8). Analysis unit: participant for the ChatGPT and Google arms, each with 60 people analyzed (p. 4, Table 1; pp. 7-8, Section 6.1, t (59)). The peer arm contains 110 participants in 55 dyads, but t (54) implies 55 observations; the source does not identify these as joint dyad scores or person A's scores, nor explain the handling of the individual baselines (p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.2; pp. 7-8, Section 6.1). A single unit covering both contrasts cannot be confirmed, so unit is null; n_units is also null because no separate observation tally is printed. The three-arm F (2, 172) is consistent with 175 observations, an inference from degrees of freedom rather than a reported people count.

contrasts.reported: MCT (flexibility): Human–ChatGPT M 15.03 (SD 3.78, N = 60), Human–Google M 12.83 (SD 3.29, N = 60), Human–human M 12.38 (SD 3.35); three-group F (2, 172) = 9.71, η²p = 0.10, p < 0.001 (Bonferroni-corrected). Mixed ANOVA: time F (1, 172) = 0.01, η²p = 0.00, p = 0.907; condition F (2, 172) = 3.80, η²p = 0.04, p < 0.05; interaction F (2, 172) = 6.08, η²p = 0.07, p < 0.01. Bonferroni post hoc within-group tests, baseline to MCT: ChatGPT t (59) = 2.48, p < 0.050, d = 0.44; Google t (59) = 0.71, p = 0.483, d = 0.11. No pairwise between-arm test printed; direction from the arm means.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Possible overlap with c471: Liu et al. (2026), Exploring the impact of ChatGPT on college students' mathematical creativity: A quasi-experimental study, doi:10.14742/ajet.10564. The c089 ChatGPT arm and c471 experimental arm have identical reported demographics: age M = 19.20, SD = 1.36; male/female 39/21; sciences/liberal arts/engineering 16/16/28; prior ChatGPT experience never/seldom/sometimes/often/always 2/10/24/23/1. They also use the same baseline and four MCT tasks, but their creativity means and SDs differ. Neither full text explicitly confirms shared participants or independence. Reuse and the number of shared people remain unconfirmed; author clarification is needed before treating these samples as independent. Possible overlap does not establish that c089 is a reanalysis.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1: Section 3.1 explicitly describes individual lottery assignment to ChatGPT, Google Search (other AI tools blocked), or human-peer assistance on participants' own MCT solutions (p. 3). The reported procedure supports lab_rct despite the quasi-experimental title/abstract; both comparisons are ai_vs_active and qualify without a no-aid arm. Criterion 2: the ChatGPT and Google arms each analyzed 60 people, already 120 people within the same experiment (p. 4, Table 1; p. 3, no-exclusion statement; pp. 7-8, Section 6.1, t (59) tests). The 110 peer participants form 55 dyads, but t (54) implies 55 observations without clarifying whose scores they represent; peer and overall analyzed-person counts are therefore null. This does not threaten the 50-person threshold. Criterion 3: two scorers marked and categorized submitted solutions and computed flexibility, fluency, and originality, with ChatGPT available during the MCT (p. 3, Section 3.1; pp. 6-7, Section 5). The unreported lottery slot configuration, unresolved peer scoring unit, and possible overlap with c471 are retained as limitations; none changes these three decisions on the available source.

one_line_finding: Students working with ChatGPT scored higher than Google users and the peer arm on flexibility (15.03 vs 12.83 and 12.38) and fluency (27.85 vs 23.78 and 23.42), and between them on originality (5.47 vs 3.88 Google and 7.00 peer); three-group F (2, 172) = 9.71, 7.91, and 18.31, Bonferroni p ≤ 0.001, with no pairwise test printed (p. 7, Table 3).
open_questions: The lottery slot configuration behind the 60/60/110 group composition is not reported; Section 3.1 explicitly states individual random assignment, which is sufficient for criterion 1 (p. 3).

The peer arm's t (54) tests imply 55 observations from 110 participants in 55 dyads, but joint-dyad versus lead-student scoring and the handling of individual baseline scores are unexplained; the peer and overall analyzed-person counts and a common outcome unit remain unconfirmed (pp. 3-4, 7-8).

Possible sample overlap with c471 remains unconfirmed despite identical ChatGPT-arm demographics and tasks; authors would need to establish independence or identify reused participants (c089 p. 4, Table 1; c471 PDF p. 7 / printed p. 45, Table 2).

The separate online appendix was not obtained. Its scoring reference tables and named correlation tables A1 and A3 are described by the main text, but its full contents remain unverified (pp. 6, 11-12, 16).
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are self-reports, not scored on the output: self-evaluation of flexibility, fluency, and originality; bias index (self-evaluation minus the within-group percentile of the actual score); interest; difficulty; effort; partner usefulness; own and partner contribution; creative self-efficacy before and after (Table 3 rows 5-18). The creativity baseline (Table 3 row 1) was produced alone before the partner phase and serves as the pre score. Table 3 p-values are Bonferroni-corrected (table note, p. 7). Post hoc power analysis only; no a priori sample size (p. 3). The ChatGPT model version is not given. Outcome IDs follow the paper's order (Table 3 rows 2-4), as in screener B; screener A numbered originality first. The related AJET paper is c471; possible sample overlap is now recorded in sample_overlap after checking both papers' full markdown conversions and the relevant PDF tables. Final review: the complete c089 markdown was read through the Supporting Information notice, and all retained creativity statistics were checked against PDF Table 3 and Section 6.1. The external appendix is absent from the saved PDF; no matching supplement was found by title/DOI filename search in the local literature folder. Python urllib requests with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 to the Wiley full-article URL and then the Crossref DOI API both failed with WinError 10013; no external appendix was inspected. The original reconciliation object is preserved as historical review evidence; its definite analyzed-person totals and common participant-unit claims are superseded by the current fields and final adjudication. Two challenge entries independently flag the same outcome-unit issue and receive separate resolutions.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O1, S1-O2, and S1-O3 were assigned a uniform participant unit despite the unresolved representation of the peer arm's observations.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Set all three outcome unit fields to null. Their measure_detail now distinguishes confirmed participant analyses in the ChatGPT and Google arms from the peer arm's unresolved joint-dyad versus lead-student scores. n_units remains null; 55 peer observations and 175 total observations are described only as implications of the printed degrees of freedom. The actual peer unit remains an open item, without affecting eligibility.

open_items.item: Original open question: quasi-experimental label versus lottery assignment. Resolved for screening by the explicit individual lottery in Section 3.1 (p. 3); the title does not leave criterion 1 unclear.

Lottery slot configuration for the reported 60/60/110 groups is unstated (p. 3). Authors could clarify allocation probabilities or fixed slots; the explicit random-assignment description already meets criterion 1.

Peer-arm people-to-score mapping, analyzed-person count, common outcome unit, and handling of individual baselines remain unresolved (pp. 3-4, 7-8). Author analysis documentation must identify whether scores represent dyads jointly or person A alone. Criterion 2 already holds from 60 ChatGPT plus 60 Google participants analyzed.

Original open question: no exact pairwise between-arm creativity test is printed. This is an extraction limitation, not an eligibility requirement; Table 3 reports means and SDs, and Table 1 supplies confirmed Ns for the ChatGPT-Google contrast. No additional evidence is needed for screening.

Original open question: no concurrent individual no-aid arm. Resolved for screening: Google Search and a human peer are qualifying active comparisons; the earlier solo baseline is not an assigned no-aid condition (p. 3, Section 3.1).

Possible overlap with c471: identical ChatGPT-arm demographics and tasks do not establish reuse. Authors must confirm independence or identify shared participants and any reanalysis. This affects sample deduplication, not whether c089 meets the three eligibility criteria.

External appendix not inspected: obtain the supplement to verify the scoring reference tables, Appendix Tables A1 and A3, and any additional contents (pp. 6, 11-12, 16). Main-text methods, people counts in the individual arms, and outcome scoring already settle eligibility.
